title: Producing values one at a time
objectives: Write a generator and use it in a loop
Compute the maximum drawdown of a price series from its running peak

screens.title: The deepest fall

explain.text: You kept one number as you walked: the best close so far. It is the **running peak**, and it only moves on days 5 and 10. The fall from it on any day is that day's **drawdown**.

screens.title: The running peak
screens.prose:
Here is the walk you just did, as code. It carries one number, `peak`, from day to day.

```python
peak = prices[0]
for p in prices:
    peak = max(peak, p)
    drawdown = (peak - p) / peak
```

steps.caption: Day 1. The peak starts at the first close, £100.00. Drawdown 0%.
Day 3. £92.00 does not beat £100.00, so the peak stays. Drawdown $\tfrac{100 - 92}{100} = 8\%$.
Day 5. £110.00 beats the peak, so `max` moves it. Drawdown is back to 0%.
Day 7. £99.00 against a peak of £110.00. Drawdown $\tfrac{110 - 99}{110} = 10\%$, the worst so far.
Day 10. A new peak, £112.00. The largest drawdown seen on the way is the **maximum drawdown**: 10%.

canvas.caption: Maximum drawdown: 10%, from day 5 to day 7

screens.title: One value per request
screens.prose:
This function hands back the peak with `yield` instead of `return`.

```python
def running_peak(prices):
    peak = prices[0]
    for p in prices:
        peak = max(peak, p)
        yield peak

g = running_peak([100.0, 96.0, 110.0, 104.5])
print(next(g))
print(next(g))
print(next(g))
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You printed the closes. `yield peak` hands back the running peak, which stays at 100.0 on the second close.
You ran the whole loop before the first `print`. The function pauses at each `yield` and only carries on when `next` asks.
You expected one finished list. Each `next(g)` gets one value, and there are three calls.

hints.text: What does the function hand back the first time it reaches `yield`?
The first `next` runs the loop for the first close only, then pauses.
First pass: peak 100.0. Second pass: `max(100.0, 96.0)` is 100.0. Third pass: `max(100.0, 110.0)` is 110.0.

feedback.correct: Each `next` runs one more pass of the loop and pauses at `yield`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the loop one pass per `next`, and note the value of `peak` each time.

byKey.ran-all: You ran the whole loop before the first `print`. The function pauses at each `yield`, holding `peak`, until the next `next`.

explain.text: A function containing `yield` is a **generator**. Calling it runs nothing; each `next(g)` runs to the next `yield`, hands back one value and pauses there. `peak` survives the pause, which is what a running peak needs.

screens.prose: `list(g)` asks a generator for values until it runs out, and collects them. A `for` loop over it does the same, one value per pass.

screens.prose:
`prices` holds the ten closes. You find the worst drawdown, then want to look at them all.

```python
dd = drawdowns(prices)
print(max(dd))
print(list(dd))
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected `dd` to replay like a list. `max` already asked it for every value, so it has none left.
A used-up generator is not an error. It simply has nothing left, so `list` collects nothing.
That keeps only the last value. A finished generator keeps nothing at all.

hints.text: To find the largest value, how many values must `max` ask for?
`max` runs the generator to its end. Where is it paused now?
The generator is finished after `max`. Asking a finished generator for more gives nothing, so `list(dd)` is `[]`.

feedback.correct: `max` used every value up. A generator runs once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what `max` did to `dd` before `list` saw it.

byKey.replay: You expected `dd` to replay like a list. `max(dd)` already took every value, so `list(dd)` gets none.

explain.text: `max(dd)` pulled all ten values, so the generator is spent. `list(dd)` then finds nothing and gives `[]`, with no error to warn you. Call `drawdowns(prices)` again, or keep `list(drawdowns(prices))` if you need the values twice.

screens.prose: You carried a running peak $M_t$ and measured each close $P_t$ against it: $$M_t = \max(P_1, \dots, P_t), \qquad D_t = \frac{M_t - P_t}{M_t}$$ This is l7's **maximum drawdown**, the largest $D_t$, now read from the prices. It is a fall from a peak to a later trough, never to an earlier one.
screens.question: Which line computes the maximum drawdown of `prices`?

options.why: That pairs the highest and lowest closes in any order. Day 3's £92.00 came before the £112.00 high, so nobody lost 17.9%.
That is the drawdown on the last day only. Day 10 is a new peak, so it gives 0.
A generator has no positions to index; it only hands out the next value. And day 7 being worst is what you are trying to find.

feedback.correct: The largest of the drawdowns, which the generator yields one at a time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The peak must come before the trough.

explain.text: `max` asks the generator for every drawdown and keeps the largest: 0.1 here. The high-minus-low line ignores the order of the days, which is the whole point of a drawdown.

screens.title: A fund's worst stretch
screens.prose: A risk report needs the maximum drawdown of a fund's daily closes. The starter reads the CSV with `csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(CSV))`: `io.StringIO` makes text behave like a file, as `splitlines()` did in l10. So `prices` is a list of floats.
screens.question: Write `max_drawdown(prices)` that returns the largest fall from a running peak, as a decimal.

widget.solution:
import csv
import io

CSV = """Date,Close
2026-03-02,250.00
2026-03-03,253.75
2026-03-04,249.10
2026-03-05,256.40
2026-03-06,261.25
2026-03-09,255.00
2026-03-10,247.40
2026-03-11,243.15
2026-03-12,250.60
2026-03-13,258.80
2026-03-16,263.50
2026-03-17,259.90
"""

def drawdowns(prices):
    peak = prices[0]
    for p in prices:
        peak = max(peak, p)
        yield (peak - p) / peak

def max_drawdown(prices):
    return max(drawdowns(prices))

prices = [float(row["Close"]) for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(CSV))]
print(f"Max drawdown: {max_drawdown(prices):.2%}")
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests. Each answer is accepted when it is within a relative $10^{-9}$ of the expected decimal.

hints.text: Reuse the `drawdowns` generator from earlier, then take the largest value.
The peak here is £261.25 on 6 March; the trough comes three trading days later, on 11 March.
Paste `drawdowns` above, then `return max(drawdowns(prices))`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first test that failed.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects about 0.0693. Getting 0.0772 means you used the highest and lowest closes, but the £263.50 high came after the £243.15 low.

explain.text: The running peak reaches £261.25 on 6 March, and the price falls to £243.15 by 11 March: $\tfrac{18.10}{261.25} \approx 6.93\%$. The later £263.50 high comes after that low, so it does not count.

ideas: A function with `yield` is a generator. Each `next` runs it to the next `yield` and pauses, keeping its variables.
The running peak is the highest close so far. A close's drawdown is its fall below that peak, as a share of the peak.
A generator runs once. After `max` or `list` has used it up, it gives nothing more.

formula.name: Maximum drawdown
formula.note: The peak always comes before the trough.

summary.trap: Reusing a generator after `max` has consumed it gives an empty result, with no error to warn you.

quiz.prose: A strategy's closes are £50.00, £40.00, £60.00 and £45.00, in that order.
quiz.question: What is the maximum drawdown?

feedback.correct: From £60.00 down to £45.00 is a 25% fall.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track the highest close so far and measure each fall from it.

byKey.hilo: You paired the £60.00 high with the £40.00 low. The low came first, so nobody lost that.
byKey.first: That is the first fall, from £50.00. The later fall from £60.00 is deeper.
byKey.pounds: That is the fall in pounds. Divide it by the £60.00 peak.

explain.text: The running peak is £50.00, £50.00, £60.00, £60.00. The drawdowns are 0, 0.2, 0 and 0.25, so the maximum is $\tfrac{60 - 45}{60} = 25\%$.

options.why: You expected the generator to start over. It never restarts; it is finished.
A finished generator does not repeat its last value. It has nothing left to give.
Python does not invent a value. A generator with nothing left signals it by raising `StopIteration`.

feedback.correct: Two closes give two values; the third request finds nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many values the generator can yield.

explain.text: The generator yields once per close, so it has two values: `3.0` and `5.0`. The third `next` finds the loop finished and raises `StopIteration`. A `for` loop or `list` catches that signal quietly; a bare `next` does not.

options.why: That is the total gain, 1.3%. A drawdown measures falls, and there were none.
A drawdown is never negative: on a new high the close equals the peak, so it is 0.
The generator still yields a value for every close. Each one is 0, and the maximum of zeros is 0.

feedback.correct: Every close is a new high, so every drawdown is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each close with the running peak.

explain.text: Each close beats the one before, so the running peak is always today's close. Every drawdown is $\tfrac{P_t - P_t}{P_t} = 0$, and so is the maximum.

options.why: The loop still ends at the first `return`, so there would be one close at most.
`next` needs an iterator, such as a generator. As written, `closes(rows)` returns one float, and `next` of a float raises `TypeError`.
Then it returns only the last close. It still hands back a single value.

feedback.correct: `yield` hands back each close and carries on with the loop.

explain.text: `return` ends the function on the first row. `yield` hands back the close and pauses, so the loop resumes on the next request. That turns the function into a generator of closes.
